name: chmod
description: Changes the access permissions of files and directories, either symbolically (u+x) or numerically (755).

flags.description: Who: user (owner), group, others, or all.
Operation: add, remove, or set exactly.
Octal mode: each digit is rwx as a sum of 4 (r), 2 (w), 1 (x) for owner, group, others.
Apply recursively to directories and their contents.
Add execute only for directories and files that already have it — ideal with -R.

examples.explanation: Sets rwx for the owner, r-x for group and others (shown via ls -l). The standard mode for scripts and programs that everyone may run.
Adds execute permission for everyone — the fix for "Permission denied" when running a downloaded script.
Private key readable only by the owner. SSH refuses keys with looser permissions.
On a web root: files stay non-executable, directories become traversable, others get no access. Capital X is the key.
Lets the group write to the directory — common for shared team folders.

about: Each file carries three permission triads (owner, group, others) of read/write/execute. For directories the meaning differs: r allows listing names, w allows creating/deleting entries, x allows entering the directory and accessing its inodes — a directory without x is untraversable even if readable.
Numeric notation sums bits: r=4, w=2, x=1. 755 = rwxr-xr-x, 644 = rw-r--r--, 600 = rw-------, 777 = rwxrwxrwx (almost always wrong).
A leading fourth digit sets special bits: 4 = SUID, 2 = SGID, 1 = sticky (see the dedicated concepts pages).
useCases: Lock down private keys and credentials.
Prepare web roots and shared directories.
Fix permissions after copying files as root.
mistakes: chmod 777 as a "fix" for permission problems — it exposes files to every user and is a security smell.
Forgetting -R when changing a whole directory tree.
Using lowercase x with -R and making every file executable.
warnings: chmod -R applied to the wrong path (e.g. / instead of ./) can break the entire system; system files have precise permissions. Always verify your current directory first.
distroNotes: chmod is POSIX and portable. GNU adds --reference and consistent -X behavior; BSD behaves the same for common cases.
